why: One word in two numbers, entered twice because the plural carries its own gloss. Nothing to confuse: a learner who knows either knows both.
A derivation, not a mix-up — аргенти́нка is the woman from Аргенти́на. The relationship is worth a root fact; a confusable link would say the opposite of what is true.
Same root, one built on the other. Belongs in a root fact, not a warning.
The adverb of the adjective. Russian makes every -ый into an -о this way, and the pattern is the lesson, not a trap.
The adverb of the adjective, exactly as есте́ственно to есте́ственный.
The imperative and the infinitive of one verb. They differ because the grammar differs, which is the thing being taught.
The same verb with по- on it. The corpus does not mark them as an aspect pair, but the resemblance is the prefix doing its job.
A verb and a particle. They never compete for the same slot in a prompt, so the spelling proximity has nowhere to bite.
A common noun and a bookish adverb. Nothing a learner is asked to produce puts them in reach of each other.
A noun and a preposition. Adjacent on paper, never adjacent in a sentence slot.
A noun and an adverb, and the English glosses share nothing. The pair looks close only in the spelling.
Both read straight off their English cognates, and national and rational are not confusable in English either. The Russian is no harder than the English it is transparent to.
One word in two numbers. A learner who knows either knows both; there is nothing to keep apart.
A diminutive, not a mix-up: ру́чка is a little рука́. Authored as a root fact on both, which says the true thing.
Same verb under a prefix. The у- is the whole difference and it is productive — that belongs in a build fact, where the prefix can be taught once and repaid across уе́хать, уйти́ and the rest.
As ходи́ть / уходи́ть: the prefix is the lesson, and a confusable link would frame a regular derivation as a trap.
Two prefixes on one root. The contrast is real and worth teaching, but as по- against при-, not as a spelling accident.
Same pair the other way round.
Both are prefixed ходи́ть. The prefix carries the meaning; a build fact says so, a confusable link does not.
The по- is the entire resemblance. Any two по- verbs of similar length collide like this, and warning about each pair would bury the real traps.
Shared prefix, unrelated roots — the same artefact as поду́мать / покупа́ть.
куп- and луч- are not close; only the по- makes them look alike.
Shared prefix only.
Shared prefix only, and the roots are nothing like each other.
Two very common verbs beginning with д-. Beyond that first letter they sound nothing alike, and a learner mixing them is not mishearing, they are guessing.
As дава́ть / де́лать: the shared letter is д.
Shared initial only.
A verb and a number that share two letters. Nothing in use would bring them together.
Shared initial only, and one is a number.
Shared initial only, and one is a number.
They rhyme, but so does half the language: -ать is the commonest infinitive ending there is.
The soft sign is shared; л and ч are not close, in sound or in writing.
ку- and then two different words. Weaker than every pair kept above it.
Twelve and nineteen are not adjacent, and дв- against дев- is a bigger difference than the teens that were kept (12/13, 15/16, 17/18).
Two apart, and пят- against сем- shares nothing but the -надцать every teen has.
